docs.title: Based Operators
docs.text:
Build a Kubernetes operator out of Pydantic models and Python, and ship it as an image and a Helm chart.

Based Operators is a model-first toolkit for custom operators. A custom resource is a Pydantic v2 model; its behaviour is Python code decorated with kopf's handlers; and the CRDs, the container image and the Helm chart that put both on a cluster are derived from them rather than written by hand.

  • Custom resources

    Describe the spec and status as Pydantic models and generate an apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 CustomResourceDefinition from them.

    How to define custom resources

    Reference

  • Reconciliation

    Attach handlers to <Resource>.on and receive the validated resource instead of a raw dictionary.

    How to write handlers

    Reference

  • Deployment

    Scaffold the Dockerfile, the CRDs and the Helm chart that deploy the operator, with health checks and optionally admission webhooks.

    How to scaffold a deployment

    CLI reference · Webhook module

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text:
1. Models — based_operators.crd turns Pydantic's own JSON Schema into the Kubernetes structural dialect, and refuses constructs it cannot represent faithfully rather than weakening them.
  2. Handlers — based_operators.handlers wraps kopf's resource-level decorators so a handler works with the typed model. Discovery, filtering, retries and patching stay kopf's.
  3. Packaging — based-operators scaffold (the based-operators console script, defined in based_ops_cli.__main__, with its logic in based_operators.scaffold) loads an operator entrypoint exactly as kopf run does, writes one CRD per resource it declares, and copies a static Helm chart that installs both. Admission webhooks come from based_operators.webhook, which the generated image imports.

Start with how to define custom resources, then how to write handlers, then how to scaffold a deployment.

docs.title: Choosing third-party deps
docs.text:
There are many aspects to consider when choosing which third-party packages to rely on. Bad things can happen, if choices are not made wisely, as perfectly illustrated by this XKCD comic:

Arguably the most important aspect is whether packages currently have known vulnerabilities. Accordingly, a whole fleet of tools and platforms exists for scanning your deps to that end, some freely usable. For looking up singular packages online, any one of these is good for use:

  • LFX-Insights: Curated info on popular code projects
  • deps.dev: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages
  • Snyk Advisor: Exhaustive info on Python and other packages

vulnerability = bug or backdoor in the source code, which can be used by an attacker to disturb the software, get unallowed access or steal data

For Python packages specifically, an open-source tool exists for scanning all your dependencies for vulnerabilities at once: pip-audit, which is in fact used within this repo.

Beyond that, package health in terms of maintenance and code quality is another important signal, that ideally serves to prevent vulnerabilities alltogether.

docs.title: Installing dependencies
docs.text:
All dependency installation should be done using uv. See the official docs for details. Tl;dr: uv add PACKAGE_NAME to add it to the core library dependencies, uv add --group GROUP_NAME PACKAGE_NAME to add it to a specific group.

See /pyproject.toml for a list of all dependency groups with descriptions in the comments.

docs.title: How to check quality
docs.text: Certain checks are run by VSCode automatically as you edit code, while others have to be run manually using VSCode UI, tasks or commands in the terminal.

docs.title: Automatic checks
docs.text:
• Linting via ruff
  • Type-checking via pyright

Discovered issues by these tools will show up as yellow or red squiggly lines underlining your code.

docs.title: Manual checks
docs.text:
Pytest test cases can be run via the VSCode tests UI (beaker symbol in left sidebar) or uv run pytest tests in the terminal.

VSCode tasks can be run via the UI by clicking ctrl + shift + P to open the command palette and then typing Run task, or in the terminal via vtr TASK_NAME. Please run all tasks with the prefixes assert-, build- and info-. Make sure none of them fail and that their printed information does not hint at any major issues.

docs.title: The full gate, in one shot
docs.text:
When the editor squiggles go quiet, run the same checks CI runs before you call a change done:

uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run pyright .
uv run pytest tests
uv run deptry .
uv run licensecheck --zero --ignore-licenses UNKNOWN --ignore-packages mypy-extensions mkdocs-typer2 -g app -g docs
uv run pip-audit .
SITE_URL="https://example.com/" uv run vtr build-docs

Every command should exit clean. pytest reporting skips is fine; failures are not.

docs.title: Gotchas that bite
docs.text:
• ruff is opinionated here — line length 100, Google-style docstrings, and max-complexity = 12. A long if/elif chain trips C901, so split it into small helpers rather than reaching for a # noqa.
  • pyright and Pydantic disagree about constructors — Pydantic types __init__ from the model's fields, so Model(spec={...}) fails type-checking even though it runs fine. Build models with model_validate({...}) or pass typed sub-models.
  • Docs execute code — pages run their fenced blocks at build time via markdown-exec. Blocks that share state need a matching session="..." attribute, or the later block sees a NameError.
  • The end-to-end suite is opt-in — tests/test_integration.py skips unless BASED_OPERATORS_K8S_INTEGRATION=1 and a cluster is reachable via kubectl.

docs.title: Types of Contributions
docs.text:
The nature of a contribution roughly aligns with the folders/files, in which it happens, and can be divided into 5 types:

  1. Refactoring contributions may add/modify any files in the repository, but are not allowed to change the public interface of modules in /src or applications in /app, nor make content changes to anything in /docs. This may be ensured by not changing any code in /tests during refactoring, though this is not a requirement.
  2. Documentation contributions only add/modify files in /docs.
  3. Library contributions add/modify modules in /src and may include Documentation contributions related to the changes in /src. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/src to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  4. Application contributions add/modify notebook scripts (in the form of Jupytext) in /app. These may be rather abstract interfaces for general use of library code, or manifest very specific use cases including elaborate explanations within the notebooks. They may include Library contributions required by respective applications. Additionally, they must add cases in /tests/app to cover at least 90 % of the contributed code.
  5. Major Upgrade contributions include larger, breaking changes to the repository, and as such are not restricted in what they add/modify. However, these contributions will trigger a major version change and thus need to be coordinated carefully with the maintainers.

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
Any contribution should be made via forking the repo / branching off main and later merging all changes back using a Pull Request (PR) (or Merge Request (MR) on GitLab). Every PR should have a single contribution type (see above), which has to be mentioned at the beginning of the PR title like so:

<Contribution type>: <Rest of your title>

If multiple types apply to your contribution, pick the one with the highest number in the list above.

For the rest of the PR description, please use the PR template.

docs.title: Developing locally
docs.text: Please refer to the local setup guide to get started with working on your local copy of the repo.

docs.title: Commits and Issues
docs.text: Larger contributions / PRs should be split into multiple commits with their own types according to the Gitmoji Spec. If a commit addresses an existing Issue on GitHub / GitLab / etc., please reference that issue via #<ISSUE_ID> somewhere in the commit message. If it resolves the issue (meaning it should be closed), add a footer line to the commit message with Closes:, Fixes:, or Resolves: followed by the issue reference. Make sure you plan ahead how to split up your contribution into commits and in which order.

docs.title: Writing Good Code
docs.text: Please adhere to coding conventions and use tooling as described in this reference. In case you plan on adding any new external (pip) dependencies, please refer to this guide in doing so. Finally, once you are ready to push your code and make a pull request, please make sure you check its quality locally first according to this guide.

docs.title: The Complete Workflow
docs.text:
The entire workflow for making a contribution goes roughly as follows:

  1. Create a fork or banch to work in.
  2. Clone your fork / branch and open it in VSCode.
  3. Install all recommended extensions.
  4. Install/update dependencies via the VSCode task update-dependencies.
  5. Make one or more commits adhering to Gitmoji Spec.
  6. Run local checks and make sure all pass.
  7. Push your commits and make a PR with a title conforming to above spec and description according to the PR template.
  8. Have a kind interaction with the maintainers in the PR comments, get approval, and merge 😊.

docs.title: How to define custom resources
docs.text: This guide turns Pydantic models into a typed Kubernetes custom resource and a ready-to-apply CustomResourceDefinition. For the full symbol list, the supported-construct table and the limitations, see the custom resources reference.

docs.title: Define the spec and the status
docs.text:
A resource is a subclass of CustomResource parameterized with a spec model and, optionally, a status model. Pass a ResourceConfig as the resource_config class variable to fix the group, version, kind, plural and scope:

from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from based_operators.crd import CustomResource, ResourceConfig, Scope, crd_yaml


class Phase(StrEnum):
    PENDING = "Pending"
    READY = "Ready"


class WidgetSpec(BaseModel):
    replicas: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=10)] = 1
    message: str


class WidgetStatus(BaseModel):
    phase: Phase = Phase.PENDING


class Widget(CustomResource[WidgetSpec, WidgetStatus]):
    resource_config = ResourceConfig(
        group="example.com",
        version="v1",
        kind="Widget",
        plural="widgets",
        scope=Scope.NAMESPACED,
        short_names=("wd",),
    )


print(crd_yaml(Widget))

apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: CustomResourceDefinition metadata: name: widgets.example.com spec: group: example.com scope: Namespaced names: plural: widgets kind: Widget listKind: WidgetList shortNames: - wd versions: - name: v1 served: true storage: true schema: openAPIV3Schema: properties: apiVersion: type: string kind: type: string metadata: type: object spec: properties: replicas: default: 1 maximum: 10 minimum: 0 title: Replicas type: integer message: title: Message type: string required: - message title: WidgetSpec type: object status: properties: phase: enum: - Pending - Ready title: Phase type: string default: Pending title: WidgetStatus type: object nullable: true required: - spec title: Widget type: object subresources: status: {}

YAML rendering

crd_yaml() renders the same manifest as YAML through PyYAML, which is a dependency of based-operators; crd_manifest() returns it as a dictionary and needs nothing beyond the core library.

The generated CRD is single-version, served and stored, and carries a status subresource whenever the resource has a status model. Nested models, enums, constraints and aliases are all carried over from Pydantic's own schema; see supported constructs for the full mapping.

docs.title: Declare a status-less or cluster-scoped resource
docs.text:
Pass None as the second type parameter (or omit it) to drop the status field, schema and subresource entirely. Cluster-scoped resources set Scope.CLUSTER, and may not set metadata.namespace:

from based_operators.crd import crd_manifest


class Gizmo(CustomResource[WidgetSpec, None]):
    resource_config = ResourceConfig(
        group="example.com",
        version="v1",
        kind="Gizmo",
        plural="gizmos",
        scope=Scope.CLUSTER,
    )


assert "status" not in Gizmo.model_fields
assert "subresources" not in crd_manifest(Gizmo)["spec"]["versions"][0]
print("Gizmo is status-less and cluster-scoped")

Gizmo is status-less and cluster-scoped

docs.title: Validate incoming and serialize outgoing bodies
docs.text:
Build resources from raw API responses with model_validate, and send them back with model_dump(mode="json", by_alias=True). apiVersion and kind are derived from the configuration and conflicting input is rejected. Omitted fields stay omitted (exclude_unset=True) while explicit nulls are preserved:

widget = Widget.model_validate({"spec": {"message": "hello"}})
print(widget.apiVersion, widget.kind)
print(widget.model_dump(mode="json", by_alias=True, exclude_unset=True))

explicit = Widget.model_validate({"spec": {"message": "hello"}, "status": None})
print(explicit.model_dump(mode="json", by_alias=True, exclude_unset=True))

example.com/v1 Widget {'apiVersion': 'example.com/v1', 'kind': 'Widget', 'spec': {'message': 'hello'}} {'apiVersion': 'example.com/v1', 'kind': 'Widget', 'spec': {'message': 'hello'}, 'status': None}

metadata is tolerant of unknown keys, so server-populated fields such as uid and resourceVersion survive a round trip without being declared.

docs.title: How to extend the CRD module
docs.text: based_operators.crd turns Pydantic models into Kubernetes CustomResourceDefinition manifests. This page is for people changing the adapter itself — if you only want to use it, read How to define custom resources instead.

docs.title: One rule to rule them all
docs.text:
Every schema starts from Pydantic's own output:

Model.model_json_schema(mode="validation", by_alias=True)

Resist the urge to walk annotations or re-derive constraints, enums, aliases and defaults by hand — that is exactly how the Pydantic schema and the Kubernetes schema drift apart. The adapter (src/based_operators/crd/kubernetes.py) makes only the dialect changes Kubernetes requires and refuses anything it cannot express faithfully, so validation is never silently weakened.

Reject, don't guess

When a construct has no faithful Kubernetes representation, raise SchemaGenerationError naming the model and the JSON-schema path. A loud failure beats a quietly lossy CRD.

docs.title: Kubernetes structural schemas: the rules that bite
docs.text: Rule Detail Every node needs a type …unless it sets x-kubernetes-int-or-string or x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields. nullable is core-only Allowed at the core, forbidden inside anyOf/oneOf/allOf/not. No additionalProperties: false It is forbidden, and additionalProperties is mutually exclusive with properties — use x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields for extra-allowing models. metadata is special Only metadata.name/generateName may be constrained, so emit {type: object}. Banned keywords $ref, uniqueItems: true, discriminator, deprecated.

docs.title: The generics trap (status-less resources)
docs.text:
class Widget(CustomResource[Spec, None]) must end up with no status field, schema or subresource. The subtle part: deleting status inside __pydantic_init_subclass__ on the parametrized class is not enough — a concrete subclass re-collects the inherited annotation from the generic base and puts status back.

The fix is to find the resolved status argument by scanning cls.__mro__ for a __pydantic_generic_metadata__["args"] of length 2, then delete the field and call model_rebuild(force=True). Note that the stored argument is None (the singleton) for [Spec, None] and NoneType for [Spec, NoneType] — check both.

docs.title: Verifying a change
docs.text:
uv run pytest tests/src/test_kubernetes.py tests/src/test_resource.py

For a real API server — it registers representative CRDs, builds the operator image and deploys it, checking establishment, defaulting, pruning, schema rejection, the status subresource and reconciliation of a live object:

BASED_OPERATORS_K8S_INTEGRATION=1 uv run pytest tests/test_integration.py

The integration suite pins Kubernetes 1.31.

docs.title: How to scaffold a deployment
docs.text: This guide turns an operator entry point into a container image and a Helm chart. For the full option list and the exact layout that is written, see the command-line reference.

docs.title: What the command needs
docs.text:
An operator entry point: a single Python file that declares, or imports, both the resource classes and the handlers. That file is loaded exactly the way kopf run loads it — its own directory is put in front of sys.path, so it may import sibling modules by their plain module names — and it is the file the image runs. app/operator_example.py in this repository is a complete one.

Run the command from the project root, because that directory becomes the build context of the generated Dockerfile: the entry point and the output directory both have to live inside it. The command is the based-operators console script of the distribution, so it needs no checkout — uvx based-operators runs it straight from the package:

uvx based-operators scaffold operator.py -o deploy

Scaffolded the Widget operator into deploy/:
  Dockerfile
  README.md
  helm/based-operator/Chart.yaml
  helm/based-operator/crds/widgets.example.com.yaml
  helm/based-operator/values.yaml
  ...

  next: docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile -t operator:latest .
  then: helm install operator ./deploy/helm/based-operator --namespace default --create-namespace

docs.title: What is written
docs.text:
Path Purpose Dockerfile The operator image: the project, plus kopf running the entry point. README.md The build, push and install commands for this particular scaffold. helm/based-operator/ A self-contained Helm chart: the CRDs under crds/, the RBAC derived from them, the deployment, and a values file holding the image.

The Dockerfile and the README are rendered from templates, so they can be read and edited like any other file; the chart is a plain chart that is copied as it is, with its text files written with Unix line endings so the result is Linux-consumable whatever platform you scaffold from, and the CRDs are generated from your models. No Python is generated: with --webhook, the image imports based_operators.webhook, a module that ships with based-operators itself.

The image installs your project

The generated Dockerfile runs pip install . on the build context, so the operator's own dependencies — including based-operators and kopf — come from the project itself. It also installs git and copies the whole context, .git included, so a project that derives its version from version control (hatch-vcs, setuptools-scm, uv-dynamic-versioning, …) installs without extra work. A project that is not pip-installable needs the Dockerfile's install step adjusted.

docs.title: Build, push and install
docs.text:
docker build -f deploy/Dockerfile -t ghcr.io/acme/widget-operator:v1 .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/widget-operator:v1
helm install widget-operator ./deploy/helm/based-operator --create-namespace

Pass the image to the scaffold so that the chart deploys what you built:

uvx based-operators scaffold operator.py -o deploy --image ghcr.io/acme/widget-operator:v1

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
kopf serves a liveness endpoint when it is given --liveness, and the generated image's command does exactly that:

kopf run operator.py --liveness=http://0.0.0.0:8080/healthz

The chart's livenessProbe calls the same port and path, so the operator is restarted if it stops responding. The command is baked into the image, and the image runs as an unprivileged user; both are visible in the generated Dockerfile.

docs.title: Admission webhooks
docs.text:
Pass --webhook when the entry point declares on.validate or on.mutate handlers. kopf refuses to start if admission handlers exist without a webhook server, so the flag is what makes such an operator deployable:

uvx based-operators scaffold operator.py -o deploy --webhook

The image then imports based_operators.webhook, the module that ships with based-operators and arms the webhook server, so no file is generated for it:

kopf run operator.py -m based_operators.webhook --liveness=http://0.0.0.0:8080/healthz

The module reads everything deployment-specific from the environment, which the chart sets: the mounted certificate directory, the port, the hostname the API server calls, and the name of the webhook configuration kopf keeps in sync. The chart itself adds a Service, a cert-manager Certificate (self-signed by default, or point webhook.certManager.issuerRef at your own issuer), and the permissions to manage the webhook configurations.

docs.title: Re-scaffolding after a change
docs.text:
The scaffold refuses to write into a directory that is not empty, so that a mistyped -o cannot quietly overwrite work; pass --force to overwrite the files it generates. The chart directory is replaced as a whole, so templates from an older scaffold do not linger. CRDs are installed by Helm from crds/ and are never upgraded by it, so re-apply them by hand:

kubectl apply -f deploy/helm/based-operator/crds/

docs.title: How to write handlers
docs.text: This guide attaches handlers to a typed custom resource defined as in How to define custom resources. For the full decorator list, the arguments a handler receives and the public API, see the handlers reference.

docs.title: Attach a handler to a resource
docs.text:
Every resource class exposes an on namespace whose members mirror kopf's resource-level decorators. Decorate a function with one or more of them; the resource selector is derived from the class's ResourceConfig, so it is never passed by hand:

from enum import StrEnum
from typing import Any

import based_operators as bk
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Phase(StrEnum):
    PENDING = "Pending"
    READY = "Ready"


class GreetingSpec(BaseModel):
    message: str
    replicas: int = 1


class GreetingStatus(BaseModel):
    phase: Phase = Phase.PENDING


class Greeting(bk.CustomResource[GreetingSpec, GreetingStatus]):
    resource_config = bk.ResourceConfig(
        group="example.com",
        version="v1",
        kind="Greeting",
        plural="greetings",
        scope=bk.Scope.NAMESPACED,
    )


@Greeting.on.create
@Greeting.on.resume
async def reconcile(resource: Greeting, patch: bk.Patch, logger: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Bring a greeting object in line with its spec."""
    if resource.spec.replicas > 1:
        patch.status["phase"] = Phase.READY


print("handlers attached to", Greeting.__name__)

handlers attached to Greeting

Stacking works because each decorator returns the function unchanged, so reconcile stays a plain Python function that is registered once per cause. Decorators may also be called with kopf's options instead of used bare: @Greeting.on.update(field="spec.replicas", param=10).

docs.title: Patch the object from a handler
docs.text:
A handler changes the resource by writing into the Patch it receives; kopf applies the accumulated changes as a JSON merge-patch once the handler returns. Setting a key to None deletes it, and patch.fns accepts transformation functions for list-based edits that a merge-patch cannot express.

Registering into an isolated kopf.OperatorRegistry lets you exercise the handler without a cluster; this is exactly the call kopf makes at runtime:

import asyncio
import logging

import kopf

registry = kopf.OperatorRegistry()
patch = bk.Patch()


@Greeting.on.create(registry=registry)
async def on_create(resource: Greeting, patch: bk.Patch, logger: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    patch.status["phase"] = Phase.READY


handler = registry._changing.get_all_handlers()[0]
print("selector:", handler.selector)

asyncio.run(
    handler.fn(
        body={
            "apiVersion": "example.com/v1",
            "kind": "Greeting",
            "metadata": {"name": "greeting-1", "namespace": "default"},
            "spec": {"message": "hello", "replicas": 2},
        },
        patch=patch,
        logger=logging.getLogger("example"),
    )
)
print("patch:", dict(patch))

selector: Selector(group='example.com', version='v1', plural='greetings') patch: {'status': {'phase': }}

docs.title: React to a single field change
docs.text:
Use on.field (or on.update with field=) to react to one path instead of the whole object. kopf parses the path and passes the field's previous and current values as old and new; every other option is forwarded to kopf verbatim:

revised = kopf.OperatorRegistry()
seen: dict[str, Any] = {}


@Greeting.on.update(field="spec.replicas", registry=revised)
def replicas_changed(resource: Greeting, old: Any, new: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    seen.update(message=resource.spec.message, old=old, new=new)


scaled = revised._changing.get_all_handlers()[0]
print("watching:", ".".join(scaled.field))

scaled.fn(
    body={
        "apiVersion": "example.com/v1",
        "kind": "Greeting",
        "metadata": {"name": "greeting-1", "namespace": "default"},
        "spec": {"message": "hello", "replicas": 3},
    },
    patch=bk.Patch(),
    logger=None,
    old=2,
    new=3,
)
print("observed:", seen)

watching: spec.replicas observed: {'message': 'hello', 'old': 2, 'new': 3}

old and new are raw values — a field value here, a whole body for whole-object handlers — so validate them with Greeting.model_validate when the typed form is needed.

docs.title: Validate or mutate at admission time
docs.text:
on.validate and on.mutate register admission webhooks. Both receive the candidate object as resource; a failing validation raises kopf.AdmissionError, and a mutation is written into patch:

admission = kopf.OperatorRegistry()


@Greeting.on.validate(registry=admission)
async def require_message(resource: Greeting, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    if not resource.spec.message.strip():
        raise kopf.AdmissionError("spec.message must not be blank")


@Greeting.on.mutate(registry=admission)
async def default_replicas(resource: Greeting, patch: bk.Patch, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    if resource.spec.replicas < 1:
        patch.spec["replicas"] = 1


print("webhooks:", [handler.id for handler in admission._webhooks.get_all_handlers()])

webhooks: ['require_message', 'default_replicas']

Side effects

Admission handlers must stay free of side effects unless they declare side_effects=True, and must respect the dryrun flag kopf passes them.

docs.title: Custom resources and CRDs
docs.text:
based_operators.crd provides a Pydantic-first base class for typed custom-resource models. It derives CRD manifests from Pydantic's own JSON Schema output, adapting it to the Kubernetes structural OpenAPI v3 dialect and refusing anything that cannot be represented faithfully.

For task-oriented guidance, see How to define custom resources.

docs.title: Public API
docs.text:
Symbol Purpose CustomResource Typed base class for custom-resource models. ResourceConfig Immutable group/version/kind/plural/scope configuration. Scope Namespaced or Cluster. ObjectMeta Common metadata model that preserves unknown server fields. source_json_schema The original Pydantic JSON Schema. kubernetes_schema The adapted structural OpenAPI v3 schema. crd_manifest A JSON-compatible apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 CRD dictionary. crd_yaml / to_yaml Optional plain YAML rendering. CrdError Base class of every error this module raises. ResourceDefinitionError The resource class or its configuration is not a valid definition. SchemaGenerationError The Pydantic schema cannot be represented in the Kubernetes dialect.

model_json_schema() on a resource returns the source Pydantic schema; the Kubernetes dialect is produced separately, by kubernetes_schema(), so no information is lost along the way.

docs.title: Supported constructs
docs.text: Construct Kubernetes representation Notes str, int, float, bool string, integer, number, boolean — Nested models Inlined object schemas Local $ref/$defs are resolved; recursion is rejected. enum, Literal[...] enum Single-value const becomes a one-element enum. X \| None type + nullable: true Requiredness is preserved independently of nullability. list[X] type: array, items — dict[str, X] type: object, additionalProperties String keys only. int \| str x-kubernetes-int-or-string: true With the documented anyOf pattern. typing.Any x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true Untyped JSON sub-tree. Field(ge=, le=, gt=, lt=, multiple_of=) minimum/maximum + exclusive*, multipleOf Exclusive bounds are converted to the OpenAPI 3.0 form. Field(min_length=, max_length=, pattern=) minLength/maxLength, pattern — Field(alias=) Wire name is the alias Validation and serialization aliases must match. Field(validation_alias=AliasChoices(...), serialization_alias=...) Wire name is the serialization alias Accepted when every choice is a string and the first choice equals the serialization alias, which is the name Pydantic emits in the schema. extra="forbid" additionalProperties: false dropped Kubernetes prunes unknown fields instead. extra="allow" x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true additionalProperties is mutually exclusive with properties. default=... default None defaults are dropped.

docs.title: Unsupported constructs
docs.text:
Unsupported constructs raise a SchemaGenerationError naming the model, field and JSON-schema path — nothing is silently weakened:

Construct Reason Recursive / self-referential models Kubernetes forbids recursive schemas. Unions other than X \| None and int \| str No faithful structural representation. set / uniqueItems: true Kubernetes rejects uniqueItems: true. Mixed-type Literal[1, "a"] No single type. Protected groups (*.k8s.io, *.kubernetes.io) Require the api-approved.kubernetes.io annotation, which is not emitted. Shape-changing serializers, computed fields, mismatched aliases, AliasPath Wire names cannot be reconciled.

Python validators remain Python validators: the generated OpenAPI schema does not reproduce arbitrary procedural validation, and no CEL is generated.

docs.title: Handlers and reconciliation
docs.text:
based_operators wraps the resource-level decorators of kopf so that a handler works with the typed resource classes from Custom resources and CRDs instead of raw dictionaries. Each resource class exposes one namespace, <Resource>.on, whose members mirror kopf's decorators.

A handler registered this way is attached to kopf exactly like its kopf.on counterpart, so kopf's discovery, filtering, retries and patching all keep working; only what the handler receives changes.

For task-oriented guidance, see How to write handlers.

docs.title: The available decorators
docs.text:
<Resource>.on.… kopf decorator Purpose create kopf.on.create An object was created while the operator is running. update kopf.on.update An essential field of an existing object changed. delete kopf.on.delete Deletion was requested; use optional=True to not block it. resume kopf.on.resume The object already existed when the operator (re)started. event kopf.on.event Every raw watch event, without cause detection. field kopf.on.field A single field changed; field= is required. index kopf.on.index Build an in-memory index; the return value is the index value. daemon kopf.on.daemon A long-running task tied to each object. timer kopf.on.timer A periodic task; interval= is required. validate kopf.on.validate Validating admission webhook. mutate kopf.on.mutate Mutating admission webhook.

Each decorator may be used bare (@<Resource>.on.create) or called with kopf's options (@<Resource>.on.update(field="spec.replicas", param=10)), and every option is forwarded verbatim to the same-named kopf.on decorator. Only the resource-level decorators are wrapped: kopf.on.startup, kopf.on.cleanup, kopf.on.login and kopf.on.probe do not operate on custom resources and are used directly from kopf.

docs.title: What a handler receives
docs.text:
kopf builds the keyword arguments; the adapter validates the raw body into the concrete resource model and adds it as resource. Everything else passes through unchanged.

Keyword Type Description resource <Resource> The validated resource model, parsed from kopf's body. api_resource kopf.Resource kopf's own descriptor of the API resource, moved here because resource is taken. patch Patch The merge-patch applied after the handler: patch.spec[...], patch.status[...], patch.metadata[...]. logger logging.Logger The per-object logger kopf provides. old / new / diff Any The detected changes; raw bodies for whole-object handlers, field values for field= handlers. body, meta, spec, status mappings kopf's raw, unvalidated views of the object, unchanged. param, retry, started, runtime, memo Any kopf's standard arguments; see kopf's Arguments page. **kwargs Any Anything else kopf adds in future releases — always accept it.

body, meta, spec and status remain available for the rare handlers that want kopf's raw views; ordinary reconciling logic reads the typed resource instead.

If the object does not satisfy the model, the handler raises pydantic.ValidationError. Because the CRD schema admits only objects that the same models accept, this should never happen in practice; if it does, it means the cluster and the operator's models have diverged.

docs.title: Differences from plain kopf
docs.text:
Aspect kopf based_operators Object argument body, a read-only mapping resource, a validated CustomResource instance Resource selector passed to the decorator derived from resource_config Resource descriptor resource api_resource Handler shape free knot of **kwargs (resource, patch, logger, **kwargs) by convention Everything else — identical: same decorators, options, causes and patching

The adapter returns the handler function unchanged (as kopf's decorators do), so decorators stack freely and the decorated name stays the plain Python function.

__pydantic_init_subclass__(**kwargs: Any) -> None

Drop the status field for status-less resources.

Pydantic resolves the generic parameters before this hook runs, but a concrete subclass re-collects the inherited status annotation from the generic base. @classmethod
def __pydantic_init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Drop the ``status`` field for status-less resources.

    Pydantic resolves the generic parameters before this hook runs, but a
    concrete subclass re-collects the inherited ``status`` annotation from the
    generic base. The resolved status parameter is therefore read from the
    parametrized base in the MRO: when it resolves to ``None`` the ``status``
    field is removed and the model rebuilt so that no status field, schema or
    subresource can leak into generated manifests.

    Args:
        **kwargs: Forwarded to the Pydantic subclass hook.
    """
    super().__pydantic_init_subclass__(**kwargs)
    if _resolved_status_argument(cls) in (NoneType, None) and "status" in cls.model_fields:
        del cls.model_fields["status"]
        cls.model_rebuild(force=True)

ResourceHandlers(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]])

The kopf handler namespace of a single resource class.

Instances are created and shared by :func:handler_namespace and are reached through the on attribute of a :class:~based_operators.crd.CustomResource subclass::

@Greeting.on.create
async def reconcile(resource: Greeting, patch: Patch, logger, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    ...

Every decorator mirrors the same-named :mod:kopf.on decorator. It may be used bare (@<Resource>.on.create) or called with kopf's keyword options (@<Resource>.on.create(field="spec.replicas", param=10)). The resource selector is always derived from the class's :class:~based_operators.crd.ResourceConfig, so it is never passed by hand.

def create[F: Callable[..., Any]](
    self, fn: F | None = None, /, **options: Any
) -> F | Callable[[F], F]:
    """Register a handler for the creation of this resource.

    The handler is invoked whenever a matching object is created while the
    operator is running. It receives ``resource`` (the validated resource
    model) in addition to every keyword argument kopf provides, such as
    ``patch``, ``logger``, ``param``, ``retry``, ``started``, ``runtime``,
    ``memo``, ``body``, ``meta``, ``spec``, ``status``, ``name``,
    ``namespace``, ``uid``, ``labels``, ``annotations``, ``reason`` and
    ``api_resource``.

    Args:
        fn: The handler function, supplied only when the decorator is used
            bare as ``@<Resource>.on.create``.
        **options: Keyword options forwarded verbatim to
            :func:`kopf.on.create`, e.g. ``id``, ``param``, ``field``,
            ``value``, ``labels``, ``annotations``, ``when``, ``errors``,
            ``timeout``, ``retries``, ``backoff`` or ``registry``.

    Returns:
        The handler function unchanged when ``fn`` is given, otherwise a
        decorator applying the same behaviour.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the resource class does not define a
            valid :class:`~based_operators.crd.ResourceConfig`.
    """
    return self._register("create", fn, options)

def crd_manifest(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build a complete ``apiextensions.k8s.io/v1`` CRD manifest for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new, JSON-compatible dictionary for a single-version CRD. Every call
        returns an independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the resource schema cannot be represented.
    """
    config = validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    schema = kubernetes_schema(resource_type)

    version: dict[str, Any] = {
        "name": config.version,
        "served": True,
        "storage": True,
        "schema": {"openAPIV3Schema": schema},
    }
    if "status" in resource_type.model_fields:
        version["subresources"] = {"status": {}}

    names: dict[str, Any] = {
        "plural": config.plural,
        "kind": config.kind,
        "listKind": f"{config.kind}List",
    }
    if config.singular is not None:
        names["singular"] = config.singular
    if config.short_names:
        names["shortNames"] = list(config.short_names)

    return {
        "apiVersion": _CRD_API_VERSION,
        "kind": "CustomResourceDefinition",
        "metadata": {"name": config.crd_name},
        "spec": {
            "group": config.group,
            "scope": config.scope.value,
            "names": names,
            "versions": [version],
        },
    }

def kubernetes_schema(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return the adapted Kubernetes structural OpenAPI v3 schema for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new ``openAPIV3Schema``-ready dictionary. Every call returns an
        independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the Pydantic schema cannot be represented in the
            Kubernetes dialect.
    """
    validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    raw = resource_type.model_json_schema(mode="validation", by_alias=True)
    definitions = raw.pop("$defs", {})
    try:
        adapted = _adapt(raw, definitions, path="", stack=())
    except SchemaGenerationError as error:
        raise SchemaGenerationError(f"{resource_type.__name__}: {error}") from error
    return _apply_envelope(adapted)

def __pydantic_init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Drop the ``status`` field for status-less resources.

    Pydantic resolves the generic parameters before this hook runs, but a
    concrete subclass re-collects the inherited ``status`` annotation from the
    generic base. The resolved status parameter is therefore read from the
    parametrized base in the MRO: when it resolves to ``None`` the ``status``
    field is removed and the model rebuilt so that no status field, schema or
    subresource can leak into generated manifests.

    Args:
        **kwargs: Forwarded to the Pydantic subclass hook.
    """
    super().__pydantic_init_subclass__(**kwargs)
    if _resolved_status_argument(cls) in (NoneType, None) and "status" in cls.model_fields:
        del cls.model_fields["status"]
        cls.model_rebuild(force=True)

def crd_manifest(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build a complete ``apiextensions.k8s.io/v1`` CRD manifest for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new, JSON-compatible dictionary for a single-version CRD. Every call
        returns an independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the resource schema cannot be represented.
    """
    config = validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    schema = kubernetes_schema(resource_type)

    version: dict[str, Any] = {
        "name": config.version,
        "served": True,
        "storage": True,
        "schema": {"openAPIV3Schema": schema},
    }
    if "status" in resource_type.model_fields:
        version["subresources"] = {"status": {}}

    names: dict[str, Any] = {
        "plural": config.plural,
        "kind": config.kind,
        "listKind": f"{config.kind}List",
    }
    if config.singular is not None:
        names["singular"] = config.singular
    if config.short_names:
        names["shortNames"] = list(config.short_names)

    return {
        "apiVersion": _CRD_API_VERSION,
        "kind": "CustomResourceDefinition",
        "metadata": {"name": config.crd_name},
        "spec": {
            "group": config.group,
            "scope": config.scope.value,
            "names": names,
            "versions": [version],
        },
    }

def kubernetes_schema(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return the adapted Kubernetes structural OpenAPI v3 schema for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new ``openAPIV3Schema``-ready dictionary. Every call returns an
        independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the Pydantic schema cannot be represented in the
            Kubernetes dialect.
    """
    validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    raw = resource_type.model_json_schema(mode="validation", by_alias=True)
    definitions = raw.pop("$defs", {})
    try:
        adapted = _adapt(raw, definitions, path="", stack=())
    except SchemaGenerationError as error:
        raise SchemaGenerationError(f"{resource_type.__name__}: {error}") from error
    return _apply_envelope(adapted)

def kubernetes_schema(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Return the adapted Kubernetes structural OpenAPI v3 schema for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new ``openAPIV3Schema``-ready dictionary. Every call returns an
        independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the Pydantic schema cannot be represented in the
            Kubernetes dialect.
    """
    validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    raw = resource_type.model_json_schema(mode="validation", by_alias=True)
    definitions = raw.pop("$defs", {})
    try:
        adapted = _adapt(raw, definitions, path="", stack=())
    except SchemaGenerationError as error:
        raise SchemaGenerationError(f"{resource_type.__name__}: {error}") from error
    return _apply_envelope(adapted)

def crd_manifest(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Build a complete ``apiextensions.k8s.io/v1`` CRD manifest for a resource.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to describe.

    Returns:
        A new, JSON-compatible dictionary for a single-version CRD. Every call
        returns an independent result.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a valid resource definition.
        SchemaGenerationError: If the resource schema cannot be represented.
    """
    config = validate_resource_definition(resource_type)
    schema = kubernetes_schema(resource_type)

    version: dict[str, Any] = {
        "name": config.version,
        "served": True,
        "storage": True,
        "schema": {"openAPIV3Schema": schema},
    }
    if "status" in resource_type.model_fields:
        version["subresources"] = {"status": {}}

    names: dict[str, Any] = {
        "plural": config.plural,
        "kind": config.kind,
        "listKind": f"{config.kind}List",
    }
    if config.singular is not None:
        names["singular"] = config.singular
    if config.short_names:
        names["shortNames"] = list(config.short_names)

    return {
        "apiVersion": _CRD_API_VERSION,
        "kind": "CustomResourceDefinition",
        "metadata": {"name": config.crd_name},
        "spec": {
            "group": config.group,
            "scope": config.scope.value,
            "names": names,
            "versions": [version],
        },
    }

def __pydantic_init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    """Drop the ``status`` field for status-less resources.

    Pydantic resolves the generic parameters before this hook runs, but a
    concrete subclass re-collects the inherited ``status`` annotation from the
    generic base. The resolved status parameter is therefore read from the
    parametrized base in the MRO: when it resolves to ``None`` the ``status``
    field is removed and the model rebuilt so that no status field, schema or
    subresource can leak into generated manifests.

    Args:
        **kwargs: Forwarded to the Pydantic subclass hook.
    """
    super().__pydantic_init_subclass__(**kwargs)
    if _resolved_status_argument(cls) in (NoneType, None) and "status" in cls.model_fields:
        del cls.model_fields["status"]
        cls.model_rebuild(force=True)

def validate_resource_definition(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> ResourceConfig:
    """Validate that a class is a complete, CRD-generatable resource definition.

    The check is intentionally repeated before every schema/manifest generation so
    that an incomplete class can never silently produce a manifest.

    Args:
        resource_type: The resource class to validate.

    Returns:
        The resource's :class:`~based_operators.crd.ResourceConfig`.

    Raises:
        ResourceDefinitionError: If the class is not a concrete resource with
            concrete Pydantic payload types and consistent wire names.
    """
    if not (isinstance(resource_type, type) and issubclass(resource_type, CustomResource)):
        raise ResourceDefinitionError(f"{resource_type!r} is not a CustomResource subclass")

    generic_metadata = getattr(resource_type, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__", None) or {}
    if generic_metadata.get("parameters"):
        raise ResourceDefinitionError(
            f"{resource_type.__name__} has unresolved generic parameters; parameterize "
            "CustomResource with concrete spec and status models"
        )

    config = resource_type._require_resource_config()

    fields = resource_type.model_fields
    spec_field = fields.get("spec")
    if spec_field is None:
        raise ResourceDefinitionError(f"{resource_type.__name__} has no 'spec' field")
    spec_model = _require_payload_model(spec_field.annotation, "spec", resource_type)

    status_model: type[BaseModel] | None = None
    if "status" in fields:
        status_model = _require_payload_model(fields["status"].annotation, "status", resource_type)

    try:
        for model in (resource_type, spec_model, status_model):
            if model is not None:
                model.model_rebuild()
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - surfaced as a definition error
        raise ResourceDefinitionError(
            f"{resource_type.__name__} could not rebuild its model: {error}"
        ) from error

    visited: set[type[BaseModel]] = set()
    _check_wire_names(resource_type, visited)
    _check_wire_names(spec_model, visited)
    if status_model is not None:
        _check_wire_names(status_model, visited)

    return config

The kopf handler interface for typed custom resources.

This module adapts the resource-level decorators of :mod:kopf.on to the typed resource classes produced by :mod:based_operators.crd. Every resource class exposes one shared namespace as <Resource>.on whose members mirror kopf's decorators::

import based_operators as bk

from .models import Greeting

@Greeting.on.create
@Greeting.on.resume
async def reconcile(resource: Greeting, patch: bk.Patch, logger, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
    desired = resource.spec

A handler registered this way is attached to kopf exactly like its kopf.on counterpart, but kopf invokes the adapted function: the raw body mapping is validated into the concrete resource model and passed as resource, while every other keyword argument kopf provides (patch, logger, param, retry, old, new, diff, meta, spec, status, ...) is forwarded unchanged. kopf's own :class:kopf.Resource descriptor, which it also passes as resource, is forwarded as api_resource instead so that no information is lost.

Only the resource-level decorators are wrapped here. The operator-level handlers --- kopf.on.startup, kopf.on.cleanup, kopf.on.login and kopf.on.probe --- do not operate on custom resources and are used directly from kopf.

def handler_namespace(resource_type: type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]) -> ResourceHandlers:
    """Return the shared handler namespace of a resource class.

    The namespace is created on first use and cached per class, so that two
    references to ``<Resource>.on`` always register into the same place.

        The :class:`ResourceHandlers` namespace bound to ``resource_type``.

    namespace = _NAMESPACES.get(resource_type)
    if namespace is None:
        namespace = ResourceHandlers(resource_type)
        _NAMESPACES[resource_type] = namespace
    return namespace

This package derives everything a cluster needs to run an operator: it loads an operator entry point the way kopf run loads it, generates one CustomResourceDefinition per custom resource it declares, and writes a Dockerfile and a CRD-complete Helm chart next to them.

The command-line front end of this package is the scaffold command of the based-operators console script, defined in :mod:based_ops_cli.__main__.

    # output directory have to live inside it for the generated commands to hold.

        operator_ref=operator_ref,

def discover_resources(module: ModuleType) -> list[type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]]:
    """Collect the concrete custom resources an entry point declares.

    Args:
        module: The module produced by :func:`load_operator`.

    Returns:
        The declared resource classes, ordered by their CRD name.

    Raises:
        ResourceLoadError: If the module declares no resource at all, or declares
            one that is not a complete resource definition.
    """
    found: dict[str, type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]] = {}
    for name, value in vars(module).items():
        if not is_resource_class(value):
            continue
        try:
            config = validate_resource_definition(value)
        except CrdError as error:
            raise ResourceLoadError(
                f"{module.__name__}.{name} is not a valid resource definition: {error}"
            ) from error
        found[config.crd_name] = value

    if not found:
        raise ResourceLoadError(
            f"{module.__name__} declares no custom resource; a resource is a "
            "CustomResource subclass that sets 'resource_config'"
        )
    return [found[crd_name] for crd_name in sorted(found)]

def is_resource_class(value: object) -> bool:
    """Return whether a module attribute is a concrete, configured resource.

    Intermediate base classes are skipped deliberately: a class that still has
    unresolved generic parameters, or that does not declare a
    :class:`~based_operators.crd.ResourceConfig`, is scaffolding for other
    resources rather than a resource of its own.

    Args:
        value: An attribute found in the module namespace.

    Returns:
        ``True`` for a :class:`~based_operators.crd.CustomResource` subclass that
        is fully parameterized and carries a resource configuration.
    """
    if not (isinstance(value, type) and issubclass(value, CustomResource)):
        return False
    metadata = getattr(value, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__", None) or {}
    if metadata.get("parameters"):
        return False
    return isinstance(getattr(value, "resource_config", None), ResourceConfig)

def load_operator(path: Path) -> ModuleType:
    """Execute an operator entry point the way ``kopf run <path>`` does.

    Args:
        path: The path of the entry point.

    Returns:
        The executed module.

    Raises:
        ResourceLoadError: If the file cannot be imported, or raises while it is
            imported.
    """
    sys.path.insert(0, str(path.parent.resolve()))
    name = f"__based_operator_script__{path.name}"
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec) if spec is not None else None
    if module is None or spec is None or spec.loader is None:
        raise ResourceLoadError(f"{path} is not an importable Python file")

    sys.modules[name] = module
    try:
        spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - reported as a load failure
        raise ResourceLoadError(f"{path} could not be imported: {error!r}") from error
    return module

def parse_image_ref(reference: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Split an image reference into its repository and its tag.

    The tag is whatever follows the last colon that comes after the last slash, so
    that a registry port is not mistaken for one: ``registry:5000/app`` has no tag,
    while ``registry:5000/app:v1`` is tagged ``v1``. A reference without a tag
    defaults to ``latest``, as ``docker build`` would.

    Args:
        reference: A Docker image reference, e.g. ``ghcr.io/acme/operator:v1``.

    Returns:
        The repository and the tag.

    Raises:
        ScaffoldError: If the reference is empty, or carries a digest rather than
            a tag, which Helm's ``image.tag`` cannot express.
    """
    if not reference:
        raise ScaffoldError("the image reference must not be empty")
    if "@" in reference:
        raise ScaffoldError(
            f"image reference {reference!r} is pinned by digest; "
            "name a repository and a tag instead"
        )
    head, _, tail = reference.rpartition("/")
    if ":" not in tail:
        return reference, "latest"
    repository, _, tag = tail.rpartition(":")
    if not repository or not tag:
        raise ScaffoldError(f"image reference {reference!r} has an empty repository or tag")
    return f"{head}/{repository}" if head else repository, tag

def write_scaffold(
    spec: ScaffoldSpec,
    resources: Sequence[type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]],
) -> list[str]:
    """Write the whole scaffold into the output directory.

    Args:
        spec: The resolved inputs of the scaffold.
        resources: The resource classes to generate CRDs for.

    Returns:
        The paths written, relative to the output directory and sorted.

    Raises:
        ScaffoldError: If the output directory is taken, or a resource cannot be
            turned into a CRD.
    """
    _guard_output(spec)
    _copy_chart(spec)
    crds = _write_crds(spec, resources)
    values = _apply_values(spec)

    context = _template_context(spec, resources)
    generated = {
        "Dockerfile": render("Dockerfile.j2", **context),
        "README.md": render("README.md.j2", **context),
    }
    for name, content in generated.items():
        _write(spec.output_dir / name, content)

    written = [Path(name) for name in generated]
    return sorted(path.as_posix() for path in [*written, *crds, values])

docs.text:
Derive and write the artifacts that deploy an operator.

The scaffold is assembled from three sources. The resource classes provide the CRD documents, which are installed with the chart. The Jinja templates under :mod:based_operators.scaffold.assets provide the generated text files. And the static Helm chart under assets/helm is copied verbatim, apart from the Unix line endings its text files are written with — Helm already brings its own templating, so the chart is not rendered here; the scaffold only fills in the image it deploys, which is the one thing the chart cannot know.

The layout written into <output> is::

Dockerfile                    the operator image
README.md                     build, push and install instructions
helm/<chart>/                 the static chart, copied with values applied
helm/<chart>/crds/*.yaml      the CRDs generated from the resources
helm/<chart>/values.yaml      the chart defaults with the image filled in

The build context of the Dockerfile is the directory the caller runs in, so the entry point and the output directory both have to live inside it.

        namespace: The namespace the operator is deployed into.

        python_version: The ``X.Y`` version of the base image.

        force: Whether existing files may be overwritten.

    Raises:

    operator_path = operator.resolve()

    # The image installs the build context, so both the entry point and the

    if not _PYTHON_VERSION_PATTERN.match(python_version):

        namespace=namespace,

def parse_image_ref(reference: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Split an image reference into its repository and its tag.

    The tag is whatever follows the last colon that comes after the last slash, so
    that a registry port is not mistaken for one: ``registry:5000/app`` has no tag,
    while ``registry:5000/app:v1`` is tagged ``v1``. A reference without a tag
    defaults to ``latest``, as ``docker build`` would.

    Args:
        reference: A Docker image reference, e.g. ``ghcr.io/acme/operator:v1``.

    Returns:
        The repository and the tag.

    Raises:
        ScaffoldError: If the reference is empty, or carries a digest rather than
            a tag, which Helm's ``image.tag`` cannot express.
    """
    if not reference:
        raise ScaffoldError("the image reference must not be empty")
    if "@" in reference:
        raise ScaffoldError(
            f"image reference {reference!r} is pinned by digest; "
            "name a repository and a tag instead"
        )
    head, _, tail = reference.rpartition("/")
    if ":" not in tail:
        return reference, "latest"
    repository, _, tag = tail.rpartition(":")
    if not repository or not tag:
        raise ScaffoldError(f"image reference {reference!r} has an empty repository or tag")
    return f"{head}/{repository}" if head else repository, tag

def write_scaffold(
    spec: ScaffoldSpec,
    resources: Sequence[type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]],
) -> list[str]:
    """Write the whole scaffold into the output directory.

    Args:
        spec: The resolved inputs of the scaffold.
        resources: The resource classes to generate CRDs for.

    Returns:
        The paths written, relative to the output directory and sorted.

    Raises:
        ScaffoldError: If the output directory is taken, or a resource cannot be
            turned into a CRD.
    """
    _guard_output(spec)
    _copy_chart(spec)
    crds = _write_crds(spec, resources)
    values = _apply_values(spec)

    context = _template_context(spec, resources)
    generated = {
        "Dockerfile": render("Dockerfile.j2", **context),
        "README.md": render("README.md.j2", **context),
    }
    for name, content in generated.items():
        _write(spec.output_dir / name, content)

    written = [Path(name) for name in generated]
    return sorted(path.as_posix() for path in [*written, *crds, values])

docs.text:
Load an operator entry point and the custom resources it declares.

The entry point is the Python file that is handed to kopf run inside the generated image, so it is loaded exactly the way kopf loads it (see kopf's own loaders.preload): the file's directory is put in front of sys.path and the file is executed as a fresh module. Loading it the same way matters, because it is the only way to guarantee that the derived CRDs cover precisely the resource classes the operator would register handlers for at runtime.

Resources are then picked from the module namespace, which covers both halves of "contain or reference the handlers": a resource declared in the entry point and a resource imported into it are equally visible there.

def discover_resources(module: ModuleType) -> list[type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]]:
    """Collect the concrete custom resources an entry point declares.

    Args:
        module: The module produced by :func:`load_operator`.

    Returns:
        The declared resource classes, ordered by their CRD name.

    Raises:
        ResourceLoadError: If the module declares no resource at all, or declares
            one that is not a complete resource definition.
    """
    found: dict[str, type[CustomResource[Any, Any]]] = {}
    for name, value in vars(module).items():
        if not is_resource_class(value):
            continue
        try:
            config = validate_resource_definition(value)
        except CrdError as error:
            raise ResourceLoadError(
                f"{module.__name__}.{name} is not a valid resource definition: {error}"
            ) from error
        found[config.crd_name] = value

    if not found:
        raise ResourceLoadError(
            f"{module.__name__} declares no custom resource; a resource is a "
            "CustomResource subclass that sets 'resource_config'"
        )
    return [found[crd_name] for crd_name in sorted(found)]

def is_resource_class(value: object) -> bool:
    """Return whether a module attribute is a concrete, configured resource.

    Intermediate base classes are skipped deliberately: a class that still has
    unresolved generic parameters, or that does not declare a
    :class:`~based_operators.crd.ResourceConfig`, is scaffolding for other
    resources rather than a resource of its own.

    Args:
        value: An attribute found in the module namespace.

    Returns:
        ``True`` for a :class:`~based_operators.crd.CustomResource` subclass that
        is fully parameterized and carries a resource configuration.
    """
    if not (isinstance(value, type) and issubclass(value, CustomResource)):
        return False
    metadata = getattr(value, "__pydantic_generic_metadata__", None) or {}
    if metadata.get("parameters"):
        return False
    return isinstance(getattr(value, "resource_config", None), ResourceConfig)

def load_operator(path: Path) -> ModuleType:
    """Execute an operator entry point the way ``kopf run <path>`` does.

    Args:
        path: The path of the entry point.

    Returns:
        The executed module.

    Raises:
        ResourceLoadError: If the file cannot be imported, or raises while it is
            imported.
    """
    sys.path.insert(0, str(path.parent.resolve()))
    name = f"__based_operator_script__{path.name}"
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec) if spec is not None else None
    if module is None or spec is None or spec.loader is None:
        raise ResourceLoadError(f"{path} is not an importable Python file")

    sys.modules[name] = module
    try:
        spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - reported as a load failure
        raise ResourceLoadError(f"{path} could not be imported: {error!r}") from error
    return module

def configure_webhook(settings: kopf.OperatorSettings, **_: Any) -> None:
    """Serve admission webhooks over the mounted certificate.

    kopf calls this once, after the startup handlers ran and before any webhook

        addr="0.0.0.0",

        host=_host(),
        certfile=cert_dir / _CERT_FILENAME,
        pkeyfile=cert_dir / _KEY_FILENAME,
        cadata=_ca_bundle(cert_dir),
    )
    settings.admission.managed = _managed()

docs.title: The webhook module
docs.text:
based_operators.webhook is the operator-side half of the admission webhooks recipe. An operator that registers on.validate or on.mutate handlers needs a server for kopf to serve them over — without one, kopf refuses to start. Importing this module arms that server, and the scaffold does the import for you with --webhook:

kopf run operator.py -m based_operators.webhook --liveness=http://0.0.0.0:8080/healthz

import based_operators.scaffold as scaffold

print(scaffold.WEBHOOK_MODULE)

based_operators.webhook

The module itself is part of the distribution rather than something the scaffold generates: templating Python is a no-go, and there is nothing project-specific in it — everything that depends on where the operator runs arrives through the environment.

docs.title: What it configures
docs.text:
Importing the module registers one kopf.on.startup handler. When kopf starts, it turns on a kopf.WebhookServer listening on all interfaces, serving TLS from the mounted certificate, and it tells kopf to manage the webhook configuration objects named for the deployment:

import inspect

import based_operators.webhook as webhook

print(inspect.getsource(webhook.configure_webhook))

@kopf.on.startup() def configure_webhook(settings: kopf.OperatorSettings, **_: Any) -> None: """Serve admission webhooks over the mounted certificate.

kopf calls this once, after the startup handlers ran and before any webhook
is needed, and reconnects the server whenever the certificate files change,
so a renewed certificate is picked up without a restart.

Args:
    settings: The operator settings kopf hands to every startup handler.
    **_: Any other argument a future kopf release may add.

Raises:
    RuntimeError: If the TLS material of the chart is not mounted, which means
        the webhook deployment of the chart is incomplete.
"""
cert_dir = _cert_dir()
settings.admission.server = kopf.WebhookServer(
    addr="0.0.0.0",
    port=_port(),
    host=_host(),
    certfile=cert_dir / _CERT_FILENAME,
    pkeyfile=cert_dir / _KEY_FILENAME,
    cadata=_ca_bundle(cert_dir),
)
settings.admission.managed = _managed()

docs.text:
Variable Meaning Default WEBHOOK_CERT_DIR Directory holding tls.crt, tls.key and optionally ca.crt. /etc/webhook/certs WEBHOOK_PORT Port the server listens on; the chart points its Service at the same port, because the API server calls the endpoint kopf advertises. 8443 WEBHOOK_HOST Hostname the API server calls — the in-cluster Service. localhost WEBHOOK_MANAGED Name of the [Validating/Mutating]WebhookConfiguration kopf creates and keeps in sync. based-operators-webhooks

The defaults only apply outside a cluster, where the chart's environment is absent. The Helm chart sets all four on the operator container.

The certificate directory must hold tls.key and either ca.crt or tls.crt; ca.crt is preferred when present, and otherwise the server certificate is advertised as its own CA, which is what a self-signed cert-manager issuer produces. Missing material fails loudly at startup rather than quietly at admission time.

docs.title: What the chart adds
docs.text:
The chart generated by scaffold --webhook adds everything around the module:

  • a cert-manager Certificate (self-signed by default; point webhook.certManager.issuerRef at your own issuer otherwise),
  • a Service exposing the port kopf advertises,
  • the RBAC to create and patch the webhook configuration objects.

kopf itself creates the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration and keeps them in sync with the handlers that are registered, reconfiguring them whenever the certificate renews.
